[[File:Kono-jinja (Miyazu) otorii.JPG|thumb|{{center|First Torii}}]] '''Kago Shrine''' (read “Kono-jinja” – also sometimes read “Komori-jinja,” though the reading “Kono-jinja” is used here) is a Shinto shrine located in Ōgaki, [[Miyazu City]], {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}. It is classified as a Shikinai Taisha (Meishin Taisha) and the Ichinomiya of Tango Province. Its former shrine Ranking under the modern system was that of a Kokuhēchūsha, and it is now one of the Betsuhyō Jinja under the Association of Shinto Shrines. It is also one of the shrines of Moto-Ise, and is known by various names such as “Moto-Ise Kago Shrine,” “Naiku Moto-Miya,” “Komori Daikongen,” and “Kago Daimyōjin.” The shrine’s head priest has been hereditary in the {{ill|Amabe clan|en|Amabe clan|qid=Q65272445|lt=Amabe Clan|1=Amabe clan}}. Although the origin of the Sōsha of Tango Province is unknown, one theory holds that this shrine also served as the Sōsha. In April 2017 (Heisei 29), the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology recognized it as one of the cultural properties that help tell the story of Japan’s cultural heritage – as part of the “Japan Heritage” story "Tango Chirimen Corridor."{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/pdf/nihon_isan_pamphlet_2019.pdf|title=日本遺産認定ストーリー一覧|accessdate=2020-11-11}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=300th year を紡ぐ絹が織り成す丹後ちりめん回廊|website=日本遺産ポータルサイト|accessdate=2020-11-11}} == Enshrined Deities == The deities enshrined at Kago Shrine consist of five figures. '''Principal Deity''' * '''{{ill|Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja|彦火明命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}''' (Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto) **Also referred to as {{ill|Amenohoakari|en|Amenohoakari|qid=Q10940411|lt=Amatenohikohikari no Mikoto|1=Amenohoakari}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Mitama no Kami|ja|天照御魂神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Mitama no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}, or {{ill|Amaterasu Kuniteru Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja|天照国照彦火明命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Kuniteru Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}, as well as {{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|饒速日命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ニギハヤヒ}}; considered the ancestral deity of the Amabe clan. '''Associated Deities''' * {{ill|Toyouke-no-Ōkami|ja|豊受大神|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|1=Toyouke-hime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyouke-no-Ōkami|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyouke-hime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to トヨウケビメ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2983724}} – also known as “Goshizunushi,” * {{ill|Amaterasu|en|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|1=Amaterasu}} * {{ill|Watatsumi|ja|海神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi|1=water deity|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1916821}} – the tutelary deity of the Amabe clan. * {{ill|Ame-no-Mikumari no Kami|ja|天水分神|1=Mikumari|2=ja|3=水分神|4=zh|5=水分神|6=sv|7=Mikumari-no-Kami|8=fr|9=Mikumari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Mikumari no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 水分神}} Various theories exist regarding these enshrined deities.{{ill|Japanese Deities|ja|日本の神々|1=Kamigami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Deities|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamigami|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – Kago Shrine entry. According to the "Tango-koku Shikishōjō Jikkō," {{ill|Izanagi|ja|伊弉諾尊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izanagi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to イザナギ}} is cited,Based on a tradition from an excerpt of the "Tango-koku Fudoki" (as included in the Shaku Nihonki). while the "Shinja Meisaichō" lists Ame-no-Mikumari as the deity. == History == Kago Shrine was founded in the 3rd year of {{ill|Jinki (era)|en|Jinki (era)|qid=Q1373210|lt=Shinkame|1=Jinki (era)}} (726) during the Nara period. According to shrine tradition, the site is the place where {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} temporarily stayed on her return journey from the conquest of the Three Kingdoms. According to the "Hakozaki Shrine Engi" (a record from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}}), in the 21st year of {{ill|Engi (era)|en|Engi (era)|qid=Q1374325|lt=Engi|1=Engi (era)}} (921) an oracle was received regarding the relocation to Hakozaki-hama (the present-day Hakozaki area of Higashi Ward in [[:en:Fukuoka City|Fukuoka City]]); then in the 1st year of {{ill|Enchō|ja|延長|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enchō|1=Enchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q97379316}} (923) the shrine was relocated, marking the beginning of Hakozaki Shrine. The oracle for Hakozaki Shrine was drawn from the oracle collection of Usa Jingu, the origin story of the Hachiman deities, which states, "Either I, from Usa Jingu, or the Hon-miya of Honami Oita is my main shrine." Even after relocating to Hakozaki Shrine, it continued to be fervently venerated as the head branch (第一社) among the Five Hachiman Shrines of Kyushu. Nearby, there are ruins of an ancient temple and the remains of the "Daibu Haiji" pagoda. At the time of its founding, the shrine buildings were located on a hillside behind the present site, but during the Sengoku period they were burned down in warfare. In the 5th year of {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|en|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|qid=Q1145058|lt=Tenshō Era|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} (1577), {{ill|Akizuki Tanezane|en|Akizuki Tanezane|qid=Q1080643|lt=Akizuki Tanemi|1=Akizuki Tanezane}} rebuilt the shrine at the current location. In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was classified as a Gōsha under the modern shrine Ranking system. In 1995 (Heisei 7), a major restoration was carried out. == Facilities == [[File:Pond in Daibu Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|Hojo Pond]] [[File:Grand camphor tree in Daibu Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|Great Camphor Tree]] * Haiden (Worship Hall) * Honden (Main Hall) **Both the Haiden and Honden were extensively repaired in Heisei 7 (1995). * Shimon (Divine Gate) * Hojo Pond – a pond used during the Hojo Festival. * The Well of Emperor Ōjin’s Birth Water * Great Camphor Tree – an estimated 350-year-old camphor tree ({{ill|Camphora officinarum|en|Camphora officinarum|qid=Q158722|lt=Kusunoki|1=Camphora officinarum}}) designated as a Natural Monument of Fukuoka Prefecture. According to tradition, it is said to be a descendant of the tree that {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} brought back from the Korean Peninsula. * Uguisuzuka – a hill approximately 10 meters high located on a detached part of the grounds near [[Chikuzen Oita Station]] on JR; according to tradition, Empress Jingū disbanded her troops here, and it is said that the place name “Oita” originated from this event. == Annual Festival == At the annual festival (Hojo-kai) held each September, the “Daibu Lion Dance” is performed. This lion dance is designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Fukuoka Prefecture. It is said to have been transmitted from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}} during the Edo period (specifically in Kyōhō 9, 1724) and, together with the “Earth-worker Lion Dance” from Hakata (in {{ill|Kaho District, Fukuoka|en|Kaho District, Fukuoka|qid=Q1156623|lt=Kaho District|1=Kaho District, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|Keisen, Fukuoka|en|Keisen, Fukuoka|qid=Q1206263|lt=Katsugawa Town|1=Keisen, Fukuoka}}), has influenced lion dances in southern Fukuoka. It is also noted that, perhaps due to transmission from Kyoto, the accompanying festival music and shouts have a nuance similar to Kyoto dialect. == Access == * Approximately a 15-minute walk from {{ill|Kyushu Railway Company|en|Kyushu Railway Company|qid=Q498366|lt=Kyushu Railway Company|1=Kyushu Railway Company}}’s {{ill|Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|en|Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|qid=Q5507634|lt=Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|1=Fukuhoku Yutaka Line}} [[Chikuzen Oita Station|Chikuzen Oita Station]]. == External Links == * [http://www.daibu-hachiman.com/ 【公式】Daibu Hachiman-gu] * [http://www.kankou-iizuka.jp/homepage/sub.asp?id=90 【Daibu Hachiman-gu】 (Iizuka City website)] {{shinto-stub}} ==Overview== ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * {{ill|Richard Ponsonby-Fane|en|Richard Ponsonby-Fane|qid=Q3246771|lt=Ponsonby-Fane|1=Richard Ponsonby-Fane}}, Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. 籠神社 | image = File:Kono-jinja (Miyazu) haiden.JPG | caption = Haiden of Kono Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Kyoto Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.58280556|N|135.19661111|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|qid=Q812767|1=Shinto}} | type = | deity = {{ill|Mikumari|qid=Q11129547|1=Mikumari}}; {{ill|honoakari|qid=Q10940411|1=Amenohoakari}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location =430 Ōgaki, Miyazu-shi, Kyoto-fu 629-2242 | website = {{Official|1=https://www.motoise.jp}} | architecture_style = {{ill|Shinmei-zukuri|qid=Q930545|1=Shinmei-zukuri}} | festival = April 24 | leadership = | designation1 = National Treasure of Japan | footnotes ={{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|{{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|qid=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}}} | location = {{ill|Miyazu|qid=Q846351|1=Miyazu, Kyoto}} | part_of = {{ill|Shinbutsu Reijō Junpai no Michi|qid=Q10444949|1=Sacred Sites of Kamigata}} }} [[File:Amabe Clan genealogy.jpg|right|thumb|Amabe clan genealogy]] {{nihongo|'''Kono Jinja'''|籠神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} in the Ōgaki neighborhood of the city of {{ill|Miyazu, Kyoto|en|Miyazu, Kyoto|qid=Q846351|lt=Miyazu|1=Miyazu, Kyoto}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|qid=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}}. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 24.The shrine is also called the {{nihongo|'''Moto-Ise Kono Jinja'''|元伊勢籠神社}}, and its ''[[kannushi]]'' has been in the Amabe clan since the [[Kofun period]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} It may be the [[Sōja shrine]] and [[Ichinomiya]] of the {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|qid=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kono Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amenohoakari]]'''|彦火明命 |}}, god of the sun and agriculture The secondary ''kami'' are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyoukebime]]'''|豊受大神|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|1=Toyouke-hime}}, goddess of agriculture and industry * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照大神}}, goddess of the sun * {{nihongo|'''{{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|qid=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi|1=Watatsumi}}'''|海神}}, water deity * {{nihongo|'''{{ill|Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami|lt=Mikumari-no-Kami|sv|Mikumari-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami|qq=}}'''|天水分神}} ==History== According to the legend of this shrine, Toyouke-Ōmikami was originally enshrined that this location before being relocated to the Outer Shrine of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]] during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|qid=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} to offer sacred food to [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], the Sun Goddess. The shrine was originally called the {{nihongo|Manai Jinja|真名井神社||}}, but was renamed in 671 by the 26th generation ''kannushi'' to "Kagomiya" or "Kago Jinja" based on the tradition that the god of worship appeared in the snow in a basket. The main ''kami'' enshrined was changed to Amenohoakari in 719 by the 27th generation ''kannushi'', but Toyouke-Ōmikami retained as a secondary object of worship.The shrine and its rituals are described in both the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' records from the early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, as a {{nihongo|''Myōjin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. It was located immediately to the west of the site of the Tango [[kokufu|provincial capital]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} The shrine consists of an upper and lower portion. The lower shrine is the [[Honden]] and is a ''[[Shinmei-zukuri]]'' structure with a cypress bark roof. It was rebuilt in 1845 and is designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Kyoto Prefecture{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} During the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} era of {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}}, the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. The shrine is located next to the [[Amanohashidate]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===NationalTreasures=== *{{nihongo|'''Amabe clan genealogy'''|海部氏系図||}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, it is considered the oldest family tree in Japan.The clan claims descent from Amenohoakari, and served as at the ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of {{ill|Tanba Province|en|Tanba Province|qid=Q954511|lt=Tanba Province|1=Tanba Province}} before it was divided into Tanba and Tango.The document records 82 generations of descent from Amenohoakari. It was designated a National Treasure in 1972.{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/201/777|title=海部氏系図|trans-title=Amebe shikeizu|language=Japanese |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |accessdate=August 20, 2020}} ===National Important Cultural Properties=== *'''{{nihongo|Biane'''|扁額}}, wooden, {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian [[File:Kono-jinja (Miyazu) otorii.JPG|thumb|{{center|First Torii}}]] '''Kago Shrine''' (read “Kono-jinja” – also sometimes read “Komori-jinja,” though the reading “Kono-jinja” is used here) is a Shinto shrine located in Ōgaki, [[Miyazu City]], {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}. It is classified as a Shikinai Taisha (Meishin Taisha) and the Ichinomiya of Tango Province. Its former shrine Ranking under the modern system was that of a Kokuhēchūsha, and it is now one of the Betsuhyō Jinja under the Association of Shinto Shrines. It is also one of the shrines of Moto-Ise, and is known by various names such as “Moto-Ise Kago Shrine,” “Naiku Moto-Miya,” “Komori Daikongen,” and “Kago Daimyōjin.” The shrine’s head priest has been hereditary in the {{ill|Amabe clan|en|Amabe clan|qid=Q65272445|lt=Amabe Clan|1=Amabe clan}}. Although the origin of the Sōsha of Tango Province is unknown, one theory holds that this shrine also served as the Sōsha. In April 2017 (Heisei 29), the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology recognized it as one of the cultural properties that help tell the story of Japan’s cultural heritage – as part of the “Japan Heritage” story "Tango Chirimen Corridor."{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/pdf/nihon_isan_pamphlet_2019.pdf|title=日本遺産認定ストーリー一覧|accessdate=2020-11-11}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=300th year を紡ぐ絹が織り成す丹後ちりめん回廊|website=日本遺産ポータルサイト|accessdate=2020-11-11}} == Enshrined Deities == The deities enshrined at Kago Shrine consist of five figures. '''Principal Deity''' * '''{{ill|Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja|彦火明命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}''' (Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto) **Also referred to as {{ill|Amenohoakari|en|Amenohoakari|qid=Q10940411|lt=Amatenohikohikari no Mikoto|1=Amenohoakari}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Mitama no Kami|ja|天照御魂神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Mitama no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}, or {{ill|Amaterasu Kuniteru Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja|天照国照彦火明命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Kuniteru Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}, as well as {{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|饒速日命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ニギハヤヒ}}; considered the ancestral deity of the Amabe clan. '''Associated Deities''' * {{ill|Toyouke-no-Ōkami|ja|豊受大神|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|1=Toyouke-hime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyouke-no-Ōkami|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyouke-hime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to トヨウケビメ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2983724}} – also known as “Goshizunushi,” * {{ill|Amaterasu|en|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|1=Amaterasu}} * {{ill|Watatsumi|ja|海神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi|1=water deity|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1916821}} – the tutelary deity of the Amabe clan. * {{ill|Ame-no-Mikumari no Kami|ja|天水分神|1=Mikumari|2=ja|3=水分神|4=zh|5=水分神|6=sv|7=Mikumari-no-Kami|8=fr|9=Mikumari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Mikumari no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 水分神}} Various theories exist regarding these enshrined deities.{{ill|Japanese Deities|ja|日本の神々|1=Kamigami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Deities|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamigami|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – Kago Shrine entry. According to the "Tango-koku Shikishōjō Jikkō," {{ill|Izanagi|ja|伊弉諾尊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izanagi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to イザナギ}} is cited,Based on a tradition from an excerpt of the "Tango-koku Fudoki" (as included in the Shaku Nihonki). while the "Shinja Meisaichō" lists Ame-no-Mikumari as the deity. == History == Kago Shrine was founded in the 3rd year of {{ill|Jinki (era)|en|Jinki (era)|qid=Q1373210|lt=Shinkame|1=Jinki (era)}} (726) during the Nara period. According to shrine tradition, the site is the place where {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} temporarily stayed on her return journey from the conquest of the Three Kingdoms. According to the "Hakozaki Shrine Engi" (a record from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}}), in the 21st year of {{ill|Engi (era)|en|Engi (era)|qid=Q1374325|lt=Engi|1=Engi (era)}} (921) an oracle was received regarding the relocation to Hakozaki-hama (the present-day Hakozaki area of Higashi Ward in [[:en:Fukuoka City|Fukuoka City]]); then in the 1st year of {{ill|Enchō|ja|延長|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enchō|1=Enchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q97379316}} (923) the shrine was relocated, marking the beginning of Hakozaki Shrine. The oracle for Hakozaki Shrine was drawn from the oracle collection of Usa Jingu, the origin story of the Hachiman deities, which states, "Either I, from Usa Jingu, or the Hon-miya of Honami Oita is my main shrine." Even after relocating to Hakozaki Shrine, it continued to be fervently venerated as the head branch (第一社) among the Five Hachiman Shrines of Kyushu. Nearby, there are ruins of an ancient temple and the remains of the "Daibu Haiji" pagoda. At the time of its founding, the shrine buildings were located on a hillside behind the present site, but during the Sengoku period they were burned down in warfare. In the 5th year of {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|en|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|qid=Q1145058|lt=Tenshō Era|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} (1577), {{ill|Akizuki Tanezane|en|Akizuki Tanezane|qid=Q1080643|lt=Akizuki Tanemi|1=Akizuki Tanezane}} rebuilt the shrine at the current location. In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was classified as a Gōsha under the modern shrine Ranking system. In 1995 (Heisei 7), a major restoration was carried out. == Facilities == [[File:Pond in Daibu Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|Hojo Pond]] [[File:Grand camphor tree in Daibu Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|Great Camphor Tree]] * Haiden (Worship Hall) * Honden (Main Hall) **Both the Haiden and Honden were extensively repaired in Heisei 7 (1995). * Shimon (Divine Gate) * Hojo Pond – a pond used during the Hojo Festival. * The Well of Emperor Ōjin’s Birth Water * Great Camphor Tree – an estimated 350-year-old camphor tree ({{ill|Camphora officinarum|en|Camphora officinarum|qid=Q158722|lt=Kusunoki|1=Camphora officinarum}}) designated as a Natural Monument of Fukuoka Prefecture. According to tradition, it is said to be a descendant of the tree that {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} brought back from the Korean Peninsula. * Uguisuzuka – a hill approximately 10 meters high located on a detached part of the grounds near [[Chikuzen Oita Station]] on JR; according to tradition, Empress Jingū disbanded her troops here, and it is said that the place name “Oita” originated from this event. == Annual Festival == At the annual festival (Hojo-kai) held each September, the “Daibu Lion Dance” is performed. This lion dance is designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Fukuoka Prefecture. It is said to have been transmitted from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}} during the Edo period (specifically in Kyōhō 9, 1724) and, together with the “Earth-worker Lion Dance” from Hakata (in {{ill|Kaho District, Fukuoka|en|Kaho District, Fukuoka|qid=Q1156623|lt=Kaho District|1=Kaho District, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|Keisen, Fukuoka|en|Keisen, Fukuoka|qid=Q1206263|lt=Katsugawa Town|1=Keisen, Fukuoka}}), has influenced lion dances in southern Fukuoka. It is also noted that, perhaps due to transmission from Kyoto, the accompanying festival music and shouts have a nuance similar to Kyoto dialect. == Access == * Approximately a 15-minute walk from {{ill|Kyushu Railway Company|en|Kyushu Railway Company|qid=Q498366|lt=Kyushu Railway Company|1=Kyushu Railway Company}}’s {{ill|Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|en|Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|qid=Q5507634|lt=Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|1=Fukuhoku Yutaka Line}} [[Chikuzen Oita Station|Chikuzen Oita Station]]. == External Links == * [http://www.daibu-hachiman.com/ 【公式】Daibu Hachiman-gu] * [http://www.kankou-iizuka.jp/homepage/sub.asp?id=90 【Daibu Hachiman-gu】 (Iizuka City website)] {{shinto-stub}} ==Overview== ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe. ''Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan''. RoutledgeCurzon (1996) {{ISBN|1-873410-63-8}} * {{ill|Richard Ponsonby-Fane|en|Richard Ponsonby-Fane|qid=Q3246771|lt=Ponsonby-Fane|1=Richard Ponsonby-Fane}}, Richard Arthur Brabazon. (1959). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SLAeAAAAMAAJ&q=The+Imperial+House+of+Japan ''The Imperial House of Japan.''] Kyoto: Ponsonby Memorial Society. [http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/oclc/194887 OCLC 194887] ==External links== {{commons category|Kono-jinja (Miyazu)}} *[https://www.motoise.jp Official home page] ==Notes== {{reflist}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Shinmei shrines}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Ichinomiya}} {{Sōja shrines}} [[en:Kono Shrine]] {{Commons category|Kono-jinja (Miyazu)}} [[fr:Kono-jinja]] [[ja:籠神社]] [[la:Kono Templum]] [[zh:籠神社]] {{wikidata link|Q705126}} [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Ichinomiya]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Kyoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Japan Heritage]] [[Category:Kokuhei Chūsha]] [[Category:Meishin Taisha]] [[Category:Miyazu, Kyoto]] [[Category:Moto-Geku Shrines]] [[Category:Moto-Ise shrines]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kyoto Prefecture]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Tango Province]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Junior Fifth Rank]] [[Category:Junior Fourth Rank]] [[Category:Senior Fifth Rank]] [[Category:Shrine receiving Tsukinami-sai and Niiname-sai offerings]] [[Category:Kanpei-sha]]

{{Short description|Shinto shrine in Kyoto Prefecture, Japan}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Kono Jinja
籠神社 | image = File:Kono-jinja (Miyazu) haiden.JPG | caption = Haiden of Kono Jinja {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=240}} | map_type = Japan Kyoto Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.58280556|N|135.19661111|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = {{ill|Shinto|qid=Q812767|1=Shinto}} | type = | deity = {{ill|Mikumari|qid=Q11129547|1=Mikumari}}; {{ill|honoakari|qid=Q10940411|1=Amenohoakari}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location =430 Ōgaki, Miyazu-shi, Kyoto-fu 629-2242 | website = {{Official|1=https://www.motoise.jp}} | architecture_style = {{ill|Shinmei-zukuri|qid=Q930545|1=Shinmei-zukuri}} | festival = April 24 | leadership = | designation1 = National Treasure of Japan | footnotes ={{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=pink|text align=center|{{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|qid=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}}} | location = {{ill|Miyazu|qid=Q846351|1=Miyazu, Kyoto}} | part_of = {{ill|Shinbutsu Reijō Junpai no Michi|qid=Q10444949|1=Sacred Sites of Kamigata}} }} [[File:Amabe Clan genealogy.jpg|right|thumb|Amabe clan genealogy]] {{nihongo|'''Kono Jinja'''|籠神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} in the Ōgaki neighborhood of the city of {{ill|Miyazu, Kyoto|en|Miyazu, Kyoto|qid=Q846351|lt=Miyazu|1=Miyazu, Kyoto}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. It is the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of former {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|qid=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}}. The main festival of the shrine is held annually on April 24.The shrine is also called the {{nihongo|'''Moto-Ise Kono Jinja'''|元伊勢籠神社}}, and its ''[[kannushi]]'' has been in the Amabe clan since the [[Kofun period]].{{cite book |last1=Shibuya |first1=Nobuhiro |title=Shokoku jinja Ichinomiya Ninomiya San'nomiya |date=2015 |publisher= Yamakawa shuppansha |isbn=978-4634150867 |language=Japanese}} It may be the [[Sōja shrine]] and [[Ichinomiya]] of the {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|qid=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} ==Enshrined ''kami''== The primary ''[[kami]]'' enshrined at Kono Jinja is: * {{nihongo|'''[[Amenohoakari]]'''|彦火明命 |}}, god of the sun and agriculture The secondary ''kami'' are: * {{nihongo|'''[[Toyoukebime]]'''|豊受大神|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|1=Toyouke-hime}}, goddess of agriculture and industry * {{nihongo|'''[[Amaterasu]]'''|天照大神}}, goddess of the sun * {{nihongo|'''{{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|qid=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi|1=Watatsumi}}'''|海神}}, water deity * {{nihongo|'''{{ill|Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami|lt=Mikumari-no-Kami|sv|Mikumari-no-Kami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-mikumari-no-kami|qq=}}'''|天水分神}} ==History== According to the legend of this shrine, Toyouke-Ōmikami was originally enshrined that this location before being relocated to the Outer Shrine of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]] during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|qid=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} to offer sacred food to [[Amaterasu|Amaterasu Ōmikami]], the Sun Goddess. The shrine was originally called the {{nihongo|Manai Jinja|真名井神社||}}, but was renamed in 671 by the 26th generation ''kannushi'' to "Kagomiya" or "Kago Jinja" based on the tradition that the god of worship appeared in the snow in a basket. The main ''kami'' enshrined was changed to Amenohoakari in 719 by the 27th generation ''kannushi'', but Toyouke-Ōmikami retained as a secondary object of worship.The shrine and its rituals are described in both the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''. The shrine is listed in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' records from the early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, as a {{nihongo|''Myōjin Taisha''|名神大社||}} and the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of the province. It was located immediately to the west of the site of the Tango [[kokufu|provincial capital]].{{cite book |last1=Yoshiki |first1=Emi |title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido |date=2007 |publisher=PHP Institute |isbn=978-4569669304 |language=Japanese}} The shrine consists of an upper and lower portion. The lower shrine is the [[Honden]] and is a ''[[Shinmei-zukuri]]'' structure with a cypress bark roof. It was rebuilt in 1845 and is designated as a Tangible Cultural Property of Kyoto Prefecture{{cite book |last1=Okada |first1=Shoji |title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri |date=2014 |publisher=Heibonsha |isbn=978-4582945614 |language=Japanese}} During the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}} era of {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}}, the shrine was designated as a {{nihongo|National shrine, 2nd Rank |国幣中社|[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]}} under the [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines]]Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' pp. 125. The shrine is located next to the [[Amanohashidate]]. ==Cultural Properties== ===NationalTreasures=== *{{nihongo|'''Amabe clan genealogy'''|海部氏系図||}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, it is considered the oldest family tree in Japan.The clan claims descent from Amenohoakari, and served as at the ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of {{ill|Tanba Province|en|Tanba Province|qid=Q954511|lt=Tanba Province|1=Tanba Province}} before it was divided into Tanba and Tango.The document records 82 generations of descent from Amenohoakari. [[File:Kono-jinja (Miyazu) otorii.JPG|thumb|{{center|First Torii}}]] '''Kago Shrine''' (read “Kono-jinja” – also sometimes read “Komori-jinja,” though the reading “Kono-jinja” is used here) is a Shinto shrine located in Ōgaki, [[Miyazu City]], {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|qid=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}. It is classified as a Shikinai Taisha (Meishin Taisha) and the Ichinomiya of Tango Province. Its former shrine Ranking under the modern system was that of a Kokuhēchūsha, and it is now one of the Betsuhyō Jinja under the Association of Shinto Shrines. It is also one of the shrines of Moto-Ise, and is known by various names such as “Moto-Ise Kago Shrine,” “Naiku Moto-Miya,” “Komori Daikongen,” and “Kago Daimyōjin.” The shrine’s head priest has been hereditary in the {{ill|Amabe clan|en|Amabe clan|qid=Q65272445|lt=Amabe Clan|1=Amabe clan}}. Although the origin of the Sōsha of Tango Province is unknown, one theory holds that this shrine also served as the Sōsha. In April 2017 (Heisei 29), the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology recognized it as one of the cultural properties that help tell the story of Japan’s cultural heritage – as part of the “Japan Heritage” story "Tango Chirimen Corridor."{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/pdf/nihon_isan_pamphlet_2019.pdf|title=日本遺産認定ストーリー一覧|accessdate=2020-11-11}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=300th year を紡ぐ絹が織り成す丹後ちりめん回廊|website=日本遺産ポータルサイト|accessdate=2020-11-11}} == Enshrined Deities == The deities enshrined at Kago Shrine consist of five figures. '''Principal Deity''' * '''{{ill|Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja|彦火明命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}''' (Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto) **Also referred to as {{ill|Amenohoakari|en|Amenohoakari|qid=Q10940411|lt=Amatenohikohikari no Mikoto|1=Amenohoakari}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Mitama no Kami|ja|天照御魂神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Mitama no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}, or {{ill|Amaterasu Kuniteru Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja|天照国照彦火明命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Kuniteru Hikoakitsumeri no Mikoto|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天火明命|1=Amenohoakari|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10940411}}, as well as {{ill|Nigihayahi|ja|饒速日命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to ニギハヤヒ}}; considered the ancestral deity of the Amabe clan. '''Associated Deities''' * {{ill|Toyouke-no-Ōkami|ja|豊受大神|lt=Toyouke Ōmikami|1=Toyouke-hime|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyouke-no-Ōkami|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyouke-hime|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to トヨウケビメ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q2983724}} – also known as “Goshizunushi,” * {{ill|Amaterasu|en|Amaterasu|qid=Q455602|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|1=Amaterasu}} * {{ill|Watatsumi|ja|海神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Watatsumi|1=water deity|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1916821}} – the tutelary deity of the Amabe clan. * {{ill|Ame-no-Mikumari no Kami|ja|天水分神|1=Mikumari|2=ja|3=水分神|4=zh|5=水分神|6=sv|7=Mikumari-no-Kami|8=fr|9=Mikumari|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Mikumari no Kami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 水分神}} Various theories exist regarding these enshrined deities.{{ill|Japanese Deities|ja|日本の神々|1=Kamigami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Deities|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamigami|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} – Kago Shrine entry. According to the "Tango-koku Shikishōjō Jikkō," {{ill|Izanagi|ja|伊弉諾尊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izanagi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to イザナギ}} is cited,Based on a tradition from an excerpt of the "Tango-koku Fudoki" (as included in the Shaku Nihonki). while the "Shinja Meisaichō" lists Ame-no-Mikumari as the deity. == History == Kago Shrine was founded in the 3rd year of {{ill|Jinki (era)|en|Jinki (era)|qid=Q1373210|lt=Shinkame|1=Jinki (era)}} (726) during the Nara period. According to shrine tradition, the site is the place where {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} temporarily stayed on her return journey from the conquest of the Three Kingdoms. According to the "Hakozaki Shrine Engi" (a record from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}}), in the 21st year of {{ill|Engi (era)|en|Engi (era)|qid=Q1374325|lt=Engi|1=Engi (era)}} (921) an oracle was received regarding the relocation to Hakozaki-hama (the present-day Hakozaki area of Higashi Ward in [[:en:Fukuoka City|Fukuoka City]]); then in the 1st year of {{ill|Enchō|ja|延長|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enchō|1=Enchō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q97379316}} (923) the shrine was relocated, marking the beginning of Hakozaki Shrine. The oracle for Hakozaki Shrine was drawn from the oracle collection of Usa Jingu, the origin story of the Hachiman deities, which states, "Either I, from Usa Jingu, or the Hon-miya of Honami Oita is my main shrine." Even after relocating to Hakozaki Shrine, it continued to be fervently venerated as the head branch (第一社) among the Five Hachiman Shrines of Kyushu. Nearby, there are ruins of an ancient temple and the remains of the "Daibu Haiji" pagoda. At the time of its founding, the shrine buildings were located on a hillside behind the present site, but during the Sengoku period they were burned down in warfare. In the 5th year of {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|en|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|qid=Q1145058|lt=Tenshō Era|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} (1577), {{ill|Akizuki Tanezane|en|Akizuki Tanezane|qid=Q1080643|lt=Akizuki Tanemi|1=Akizuki Tanezane}} rebuilt the shrine at the current location. In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was classified as a Gōsha under the modern shrine Ranking system. In 1995 (Heisei 7), a major restoration was carried out. == Facilities == [[File:Pond in Daibu Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|Hojo Pond]] [[File:Grand camphor tree in Daibu Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|250px|Great Camphor Tree]] * Haiden (Worship Hall) * Honden (Main Hall) **Both the Haiden and Honden were extensively repaired in Heisei 7 (1995). * Shimon (Divine Gate) * Hojo Pond – a pond used during the Hojo Festival. * The Well of Emperor Ōjin’s Birth Water * Great Camphor Tree – an estimated 350-year-old camphor tree ({{ill|Camphora officinarum|en|Camphora officinarum|qid=Q158722|lt=Kusunoki|1=Camphora officinarum}}) designated as a Natural Monument of Fukuoka Prefecture. According to tradition, it is said to be a descendant of the tree that {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū|1=Empress Jingū}} brought back from the Korean Peninsula. * Uguisuzuka – a hill approximately 10 meters high located on a detached part of the grounds near [[Chikuzen Oita Station]] on JR; according to tradition, Empress Jingū disbanded her troops here, and it is said that the place name “Oita” originated from this event. == Annual Festival == At the annual festival (Hojo-kai) held each September, the “Daibu Lion Dance” is performed. This lion dance is designated as an Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Fukuoka Prefecture. It is said to have been transmitted from {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|en|Iwashimizu Hachimangū|qid=Q710098|lt=Iwashimizu Hachimangū|1=Iwashimizu Hachimangū}} during the Edo period (specifically in Kyōhō 9, 1724) and, together with the “Earth-worker Lion Dance” from Hakata (in {{ill|Kaho District, Fukuoka|en|Kaho District, Fukuoka|qid=Q1156623|lt=Kaho District|1=Kaho District, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|Keisen, Fukuoka|en|Keisen, Fukuoka|qid=Q1206263|lt=Katsugawa Town|1=Keisen, Fukuoka}}), has influenced lion dances in southern Fukuoka. It is also noted that, perhaps due to transmission from Kyoto, the accompanying festival music and shouts have a nuance similar to Kyoto dialect. == Access == * Approximately a 15-minute walk from {{ill|Kyushu Railway Company|en|Kyushu Railway Company|qid=Q498366|lt=Kyushu Railway Company|1=Kyushu Railway Company}}’s {{ill|Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|en|Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|qid=Q5507634|lt=Fukuhoku Yutaka Line|1=Fukuhoku Yutaka Line}} [[Chikuzen Oita Station|Chikuzen Oita Station]]. == External Links == * [http://www.daibu-hachiman.com/ 【公式】Daibu Hachiman-gu] * [http://www.kankou-iizuka.jp/homepage/sub.asp?id=90 【Daibu Hachiman-gu】 (Iizuka City website)] {{shinto-stub}} ==Overview== ==References== * Plutschow, Herbe.
